alt: “Chairs” is a topic tied to one kind of product. “Ergonomics” is a concept that applies to chairs, keyboards, door handles and phone apps alike, so what you learn transfers to the next project.
caption: Concepts travel between projects; topics do not.

alt: Four cards. Communication: the product communicates with its user and the designer communicates through the folder. Communities: design for groups and ask who is left out. Development: a product changes over generations, and your own solution develops from sketch to prototype. Systems: parts work together as input, process and output, often with feedback.
caption: Each key concept prompts a different question about a design.

alt: A plant-watering system: the input is a soil moisture sensor reading, a microcontroller compares it with a set level, and the output opens a valve so water flows. Feedback: as the reading rises the valve closes. A flat sensor battery would stop the whole system.
caption: Describe a system as input, process and output, then trace the feedback.

alt: A bell-shaped distribution of a body measurement with the 5th and 95th percentiles marked and the middle 90% of users shaded. Reach problems such as a shelf use the 5th percentile, clearance problems such as a doorway use the 95th, and adjustable products cover the full range. Designing for the 50th percentile fits almost no one well.
caption: Reach: design for the small user. Clearance: design for the large user.

alt: An adjustable stool set from fictional popliteal heights of 380 mm (5th percentile) and 460 mm (95th), plus 25 mm for shoes: it adjusts from 405 mm to 485 mm, a travel of 80 mm. A handle is a clearance problem: the 95th-percentile hand breadth of 88 mm plus a 10 mm allowance gives a 98 mm grip.
caption: Add allowances to the percentile values to turn body data into design sizes.

alt: Adaptation examples, each from original to new need to change: plant burrs to hook-and-loop fastening, standard cutlery to thick soft handles for limited grip, and a website rearranging for a small screen. Invention creates something new that may never be adopted; innovation puts a new idea into successful use, either incrementally (a suitcase gains wheels) or radically (touchscreens replace keypads).
caption: Adaptation reworks an existing design; innovation is a new idea that gets used.

alt: For a lunch-queue unit, the key concept systems, related concepts ergonomics and sustainability, and the global context globalization and sustainability combine into a statement of inquiry. “We will design a better lunch queue” is weak; “Systems designed around how people actually move and wait use space, time and resources more efficiently” is stronger and transfers to other settings.
caption: One sentence that links the concepts and context and would hold for other products.

alt: Three question types for a seating unit: factual questions have a checkable answer, such as a 95th-percentile hand breadth; conceptual questions ask how ideas connect, such as how ergonomic data changes who can use a product; debatable questions invite disagreement, such as whether a public bench should prioritise comfort. A debatable question must be arguable both ways with evidence.
caption: Write two or three of each type: factual for research, conceptual and debatable for depth.
